utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Today is Wednesday, and I would like to greet the witness, as well as all the accused here, the Defence counsel and the OTP, as well as all those who assist us in this courtroom, including the court reporter who provided a tremendous performance yesterday because she worked both in the morning and in the afternoon session. Thank you very much to her. We are going to start now with the cross-examination of the witness that will be conducted by Mr. Bos, and good morning to Mr. Bos. And you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everybody in and around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Perkovic. Mr. Perkovic, I'm going to have a couple of questions for you, and I've organized it in such a way that will go in chronological order through the evidence. So I'll start with some questions on your background. Now, you testified that in 1988/1989 you were president of the youth organization of the Socialist Federal Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in 1988.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Can you tell us, who was your predecessor in that organization?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My predecessor was Mr. Milos Jelic. He was the president of the youth organization in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Do you know whether Mr. Jadranko Prlic was ever president of this organization?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the level of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I know that he was not the president of the youth organization at that level ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: When did you first meet Mr. Jadranko Prlic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We met in 1988, so the first time we met was when I was the president of the youth organization of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And what was Mr. Prlic's function at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the president of the Executive Board in the Assembly of the Mostar municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And how well -- was this just one meeting, or did you have more meetings during that period with Mr. Prlic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We - I as the president - had to deal with the issue of the employment of two of our colleagues whose term of office had expired, they were from Mostar, and that was the reason why I met with Mr. Prlic who was at the time the president of the Executive Board of the Municipal Assembly. He asked me to help him, but I think that we only met just a few times in the period up to the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So -- and then the next time that you worked closely with Mr. Prlic was during the war when you were a member of -- president of the Commission of Regulation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's when I met him for the first time in this first period when I came to Herzegovina in August 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: During that period of time, were you well acquainted with Mr. Prlic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was just an acquaintance.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Did you ever work with Mr. Prlic after -- after the war, after the Dayton Agreements, in any function?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the Dayton Agreements, up until my arrival in the foreign ministry, I had two jobs, as I've already said. I was the deputy minister of justice and administration in the last cabinet of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina; and, at the same time, Mr. Prlic was also a member of that cabinet, government, which means that for a while, for about a year and a half, we were in the same government. He was the minister and I was a deputy minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's go back again to 1990. This was a time when you ran for the BiH Presidency as member of the SDP; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Presidency of the SDP nominated me for this position, member of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And is it correct that Mr. Ivo Komsic was the leader of the SDP at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The president of the SDP in BiH was Mr. Nijaz Durakovic; Ivo Komsic was a member of the SDP Presidency. Together with me, or I together with him, we were candidates for the post in the BiH Presidency representing the Croatian people.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, you've testified on Monday that your involvement with the SDP party in 1992 subsided, that's the word that was in the transcript. What was the reason for this? Can you explain how you were -- got away from that party?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After leaving Sarajevo, I went to Livno where every work stopped, and the SDP branch there virtually ceased to exist. And throughout this time, from 1992 until 1995, for all intents and purposes in the area where I was, which is the area of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, any kind of a party politics virtually ceased to exist. So that was one of the reasons, a key reason. And upon my return to Sarajevo, the circumstances and the people in the party changed substantially, and I no longer saw myself as a member of that political party.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, from 1990 to April 1992, you were the assistant minister for administration in the BiH government in Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And then you left Sarajevo in April 1992. I'm just wondering, when you left in April, did you resign as assistant minister or were you fired from that job? Can you explain what happened in relation to that function.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked my minister to approve my departure from Sarajevo because my family, my wife and my son who was one year old, were in Livno, and I asked for some short time off to take care of my family, to find some accommodation for them, and in general to see to their bare necessities. When I left Sarajevo, it was not my intention to leave Sarajevo for good, at the time, in April, when I decided to leave Sarajevo for a couple of days or maybe a week or two. At the time when I left, Sarajevo was not under siege yet, so I was able to leave Sarajevo by train. I went by train to Visoko. The town was not blocked yet. But a few days after I left, Sarajevo was completely blocked. It was impossible to go back. In an unorganized manner, it was possible to do so, only if the trip back were organized by UNPROFOR or in some other way. I knew that as a Croat I didn't stand a chance of passing through the blockade without being arrested by the Serb forces that besieged the town. And then in August 1992, for reasons that I've already explained, I went back to Sarajevo --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and, well, you know how the story progresses from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Because in that meantime, before you go back to Sarajevo in August 1992, you do some work for the Livno municipality and then later on you become involved in drafting legislation for the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. I'm just wondering, was it not a problem for you that you still had a position in Sarajevo while doing these other jobs? Did you not consider that a problem? Did you inform, for example, the Sarajevo -- people in Sarajevo? I don't know if it was possible. Can you explain to us.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout that time, up until my return to Sarajevo in August, all those tasks that I was supposed to do, my job, I did as part of my work obligation because that was my wartime assignment. I was not paid for the work that I did; and as every other person under that kind of obligation, I merely performed the tasks that were given to me in accordance with my wartime assignment. So, throughout this period my -- I was employed with the Ministry of Justice and Administration in Sarajevo. I think that was the case up until October 1992, when my employment was terminated in the Ministry of Justice and Administration, at least that is what I can see in my work record booklet.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So when you came back in August 1992 in Sarajevo, your position was -- you were still the assistant minister, and it was only in October 1992 that somebody else took that job; is that how I should understand it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. When I returned to Sarajevo in August, my post, that of an assistant minister, was occupied by another person. Another person was appointed. And I was offered to retain employment but at a lower level, and I did not accept that offer, so that in the end, I think it was in early October, my employment was terminated.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, just one question about your functions after the war. You've testified that from 1995 until 1999, you were chef de cabinet for the president of the BiH Federation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I just want to make a small note. In that period, the president and the vice-president of the Federation rotated over a period of one year. So I was always the chef de cabinet -- or rather, one year I was the chef de cabinet of this person who was the president of the Federation, and then the next year I was again the chef de cabinet of the same person, but at that time he was the vice-president of the Federation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Very well. Now, during this period, were you ever a member of the federal commission of missing persons, the Bosnian Croat side?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commission for missing persons at that time had professionals working there and also representatives of other institutions who were also on the commission. I was never a professional member of the commission, but for a while I represented the state institutions that nominated me and I was a member of that commission in that capacity.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And did you work with Berislav Pusic in that capacity?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I worked with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have to object. This goes beyond the scope of the examination-in-chief. I never heard any mention of Mr. Berislav Pusic's work in the examination-in-chief, and that is why I never asked any questions in my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Bos, during the examination-in-chief, the situation of Mr. Pusic was never mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, I don't intend to take this further. I just want to -- I think it's important for the Chamber to know that this witness, you know, worked together with Berislav Pusic. That's the only information that I intend to reveal here. I'm not taking this any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Please move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Mr. Perkovic, you've stated that in April 1992 you left Sarajevo by train because, you know, the siege hadn't started. Now, in August 1992, when you got back to Sarajevo, it's correct that you flew back on an UNPROFOR plane; am I right in understanding? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And at this time you flew together with the president, Pelivan, who was also in this plane. Did Mr. Pelivan at that time -- was he in Herzegovina and was he flying back to Sarajevo just like you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, he was in Herzegovina, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, is it correct that during this period and also throughout the war that UNPROFOR planes could go in and out of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the period while I was in Sarajevo, that was from August until November, the end of November, UNPROFOR planes could not fly for a month and a half because one of those planes had been downed; and after this incident, all flights were suspended. It was possible that there were longer or shorter breaks in this service, but I recall this particular suspension very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Very well. So there may have been suspensions, but all in all, I mean, there were UNPROFOR flights going in and out of Sarajevo; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And did it happen more often that government officials from the BiH government would, you know, use these planes in order to move around in Bosnia-Herzegovina or outside Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, can we be a little more precise of government officials. I mean, it's one thing for Mr. Izetbegovic; it is another for functionaries, you know, simple bureaucrats, who make the system move.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, let me put it this way, Mr. Perkovic, you were on this plane going to Sarajevo in August 1992. Was that exceptional that you could take this plane to Sarajevo on an UNPROFOR plane, or did other officials on your level on occasion fly with UNPROFOR flights?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I'm concerned, the prime minister put me on this flight because on the list of Mr. Pelivan's associates, they put my name on it. I think that lower-level officials could not get on to those UNPROFOR flights without the backing of the highest institutions of Bosnia-Herzegovina, of the state. There was a clear procedure in place, and it was clearly defined who can ask to use the planes to get into Sarajevo and Bosnia-Herzegovina and to get out of Bosnia and Herzegovina. What you asked me about, it was impossible to use those planes to fly from one place to another within Bosnia-Herzegovina; they were not used for this purpose at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, when you went back to Sarajevo in August 1992, I think you stayed there until about December 1992, and then you again went to Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remained there up until the end of November 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: How did you get out of Sarajevo at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A liaison officer, Vladimir Pogarcic, he was in charge of liaising with UNPROFOR, he put me on the list as a member of the delegation that was leaving Sarajevo to attend a meeting of some sort, a conference. So that's how I got out of Sarajevo, as a member of that delegation, although in effect I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And where did that plane fly to?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Sarajevo-Split, so I got off at Split, Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, on Monday you testified that throughout the war, there was contact between the republican institutions in Sarajevo and the institutions of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and later the Republic of Herceg-Bosna. Do you recall that evidence?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, one of the things you stated was the following, and I'm reading from the transcript of the 1st of September, page 89: "It was the nature of my work, and I was working with the regulation commission at the time. I was probably among the people who had the least contacts of that nature. People working across the various departments were probably encountering more opportunities to meet all sorts of people working with the BiH administration. My own experience based on these contacts was very positive and satisfying in every way." Do you recall this evidence?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, did these officials of the BiH administration from Sarajevo, did they come to Herceg-Bosna or did officials from Herceg-Bosna also go to Sarajevo when these meetings took place throughout the war? Where did they meet?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most parts, those meetings took place outside of Bosnia and Herzegovina, for instance, in Zagreb where the Government of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the first months of the war had its office in the Palace Hotel in Zagreb. Apart from that, most of the meetings took place in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. I don't think that in the first months of the war that any of the HZ HB officials was able to get into Sarajevo except in the way that I described, by using UNPROFOR; and to my knowledge, this did not happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So you say the first months of the war. Did that change later then? Did there come a time that it was possible to get into Sarajevo, and can you tell us around what time that was?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At a later stage, this regime for getting into Sarajevo by plane, by UNPROFOR planes, was a bit more lax. And it was also possible to get into Sarajevo by land because at one point - I can't recall when it was - convoys started getting in and out of Sarajevo by land, and they brought in supplies, food, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: But I'm just going to press you on this one. When you say "at a later stage," can you give an approximate month or --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I left Sarajevo in August, and I know that up until that period it was possible to get in and out only by air. I know, I recall, that later on those convoys were able to get in and out of Sarajevo by land. I think it started sometime in 1993, but I did not have anything to do with this at all, so I'm just telling you this on the basis of my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Very well. And besides meetings between the BiH administration and the Herzegovina administration, was it possible to have contacts in other ways, for example, by telephone or by fax or by satellite phone? Was it possible to communicate?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, in July -- or rather, in September 1992, there were three satellite phones in Sarajevo. One was kept in the office of the prime minister of the republic, another was in the office of the president of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the third was in the offices of a businessman who used to be an interior minister of Bosnia-Herzegovina. To my knowledge, those were the only three satellite phones in existence in Sarajevo at the time. There were also ham radio operators, and I tried to get in touch over ham radio to let my family know that I was alive because my family had not heard from me for three months.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And did you manage to get this touch with them?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that I sent -- or rather, the messages that those ham --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- tried to send --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- never reached Livno.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I'm getting some French translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: But it seems that the message never got through; that's I think what we can read from the transcript. Now, you've testified on Monday that you also had several meetings with BiH government representatives in 1993. You spoke about the assistant minister of justice and the assistant minister of interior, and then you also referred to a meeting that you had with Mr. Ivo Komsic in Medjugorje; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Can you tell us again, first of all, approximately when did that meeting take place and what was discussed at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you asking me about the meeting with Mr. Komsic?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yes, I am, yes.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had only one meeting with Mr. Komsic at the Annamaria Hotel in Medjugorje. I was invited to that meeting because a message had been left for me that I found as I went back to my office that some individuals were inquiring after me. When I came to the Annamaria Hotel, that's the name of the hotel, I met Father Petar Andjelovic and a member of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mr. Komsic. They told me that they came to have a word with me because in Sarajevo, there was a vacant post for a member of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the post that was reserved for a Croat representative. They told me that on the basis of the votes I received, I was the next one in line who was supposed to take over that position. They told me also that they had just come from Zagreb where they had informed President Tudjman of this intention of theirs. He, the president, was not acquainted with me and had no objection to that. They also told me that they had agreed on this with President Izetbegovic and that they were only waiting for my consent. My reply was that I was taken by surprise by this offer because due to poor communications, I wasn't aware of the fact that Mr. Kljuic had resigned from his post as member of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I asked them to give me some time to think it over. After a short while, after I mulled it over, I told them that I had the courage to take that job on, on condition that this matter be discussed with the highest officials of Herceg-Bosna, primarily with Mr. Boban. My position was that I wanted to make sure that this was agreed upon and that guarantees would be provided for my family that was in Herceg-Bosna. To my knowledge, this agreement was reached; however, it was never implemented. I did not regret it much because the wartime situation was quite difficult. This was not implemented for the following reason: When the Croat side in Herceg-Bosna consented to my being engaged in this way, Mr. Kljuic changed his mind, re-assumed his post as member of the Presidency because he went back to Sarajevo, and overnight he had been re-appointed. With hindsight, I think that this was a mere bluff based on their expectations that I would not be accepting the post.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Do you know why Mr. Kljuic changed his mind? Did you find out? Did it have anything to do with your being -- that, you know, with the fact that you would take his position?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard stories that were hearsay. I never heard a story from Mr. Kljuic. The story was that some other deal had been reached with Mr. Izetbegovic, most probably on the basis of their assessment of Mr. Kljuic being more forthcoming for cooperation than I.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Just one last question: When did you have that meeting with Mr. Komsic in Medjugorje, approximately what month in 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the exact recollection. I think it was sometime in October 1993. As for these talks that were held with me about me taking the position in the Presidency of BH, Mr. Ljubo Lucic published a book which contains a detailed description of these meetings and the discussions taking place in Sarajevo which I was not aware of at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Very well. Okay. Well, we'll leave this topic aside. I'm now going to ask you again some questions about the period 1991, dealing specifically with the period prior to the February 1992 referendum, when you were the assistant minister of administration in the BiH government. And I'm going to ask the usher to put a quote from your evidence in the Kordic case on the ELMO in relation to this period. It's correct that you testified in the Kordic case in June 2000, Mr. Perkovic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, on the screen, there will appear a quote from your evidence in that case, and it's both in the English and in the B/C/S language.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: The reference is on the bottom of the quote.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: May we have the page number, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: The page number is 20665, and it's the 7 June session.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, it's on the ELMO, but maybe I'll just read out the quote and I'll do it slowly. "Q. Can you tell me, please, did you know Mate Boban's position on the future of the territory of Herceg-Bosna? What was your understanding of his position, if you knew?" Then your answer: "It is important to distinguish between two different periods here, the period of the proclamation of Bosnia-Herzegovina as an independent state in carrying out the referendum and, on the other hand, the period after the referendum was carried out and after Bosnia-Herzegovina was proclaimed an independent state. "In the period up to the proclamation of Bosnia-Herzegovina as an independent state, the Croat political leaders of Bosnia-Herzegovina had different alternatives in terms of viewing the Bosnian-Herzegovinian crisis and also the fate of the Croat people as a constituent people in this Republic. "After the proclamation, after the proclamation of Bosnia-Herzegovina as an independent state, Mr. Boban signed three peace plans on behalf of the Croats of Bosnia-Herzegovina: The Cutileiro Plan, the Vance-Owen Plan, and the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan. All these plans included that area into the territory of the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina." Do you recall this testimony?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your reading it out has refreshed my memory, and I do believe that this is what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to focus on when you talk about the different alternatives in terms of viewing the Bosnia-Herzegovina crisis that were discussed by the Croat people in 1991. Can you elaborate a bit on this, on what kind of alternatives were proposed by the Croat leaders during this period?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this statement of mine, I referred to Croatian politicians. There was a whole spectrum of Croatian politicians who were from different political parties which viewed the position of the Croat people in Bosnia-Herzegovina differently. Thus, for instance, the Croatian politicians from the SDP, the Social Democratic Party; and I counted myself as one of those, Mr. Komsic, and others. We believed that Bosnia-Herzegovina in the process of the break-up of Yugoslavia was supposed to be an independent state with a decentralised administration within Bosnia and Herzegovina with more efficient structures, state agencies, and so on. The Croat politicians from the HDZ probably held different views on the issue of decentralisation, which was formulated in their aspirations for the so-called cantonisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The politicians of the Croat people from some other parties, such as the party of Mr. Markovic, the erstwhile prime minister of Yugoslavia, evidently held the following view, to my knowledge: That the internal system of the republic should be retained in the model that was previously espoused; that's to say, to have the centralised republican authorities and then local authorities on the other side. In a word, the Croat politicians held different views on what the future system of Bosnia-Herzegovina should be, and this large spectrum of positions was later manifested in the development of the Constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina after the multi-party elections were held.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Was one of the views the idea of establishing the borders of a Croatian Banovina, meaning that part of Bosnia-Herzegovina would actually be -- become part of Croatia and following the borders of an entity which was called the Croatian Banovina? Do you recall whether that idea was also being expressed as an population; and if so, by whom?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the period up to the start of the war, I attended several meetings of the Croatian Democratic Party in the capacity of the assistant minister, as a leader of the Croat people in that ministry. To my knowledge, none of these meetings discussed that particular idea, that particular solution. Therefore, I attended only a couple of such meetings, but none of them discussed the option of the Croatian Banovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: But are you acquainted with or are you familiar with this term "Banovina"? Was that something that came up during that period? I mean, let me ask you this: Do you know the term the "Banovina"? Was it something that was discussed during this period either in the newspapers, not necessarily in meetings that you attended, but in general as something that was an issue discussed by some Croat political leaders?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of such discussions. As for the term, I'm quite familiar with it because I am familiar with the history of that general region, and, in particular, of the history of the Croat people in the territory of the former SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So is it your evidence that you never -- during this period, you never read in the newspaper or you never saw on television Croat leaders discussing this particular idea of the Banovina? Is that your evidence, that you'd never heard about that in 1991?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your question did not refer to newspapers, and I didn't even talk about anyone mentioning the term in the press or not. I told you that none of the official meetings I attended in that period of time included discussions on the Croatian Banovina. We received in Bosnia-Herzegovina all the papers, newspapers, published in Croatia and Serbia, including all the Herzegovina publications. It was difficult to read through all that and be aware of everything, and I do not exclude the possibility that someone may have discussed it and that it was published in the newspapers. I was referring to the conduct of the bodies and agencies that formed part of the government, of the state.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Do you know which political parties supported this idea of the Banovina, or can you mention any name of somebody who supported this idea?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Objection to the form of the question. He never indicated that a particular party supported. So if he wishes to rephrase it as to whether a political party supported it, that's fine; but the way the question is phrased, it assumes a fact that's not in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, I'm happy to rephrase it in the way that Mr. Karnavas has suggested it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So do you know whether there was a political party supporting this idea and during this period?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of a single political party in Bosnia-Herzegovina that supported this idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move to another topic. We had a long discussion on Monday about the terms "teritorija" and "podrucje," and I'd like to come back to that topic which I'm afraid we'll have to do one more time. Now, let me try to summarize what you testified about this. You seem to be saying that there is a legal distinction between the term "teritorija" and "podrucje," and you're saying "teritorija" refers to an area in which a government exercises authority, as opposed to the term "podrucje" which is translated more as area and which can be an area within a territory. Would that be a good summary of your evidence?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since you're asking me, I'll try and repeat what I said on Monday. I said, first of all, that there is a legal and layman's understanding of these terms, and the two or not the same. When I spoke of territory, I said that in my view, territory is an area with clearly defined borders over which sovereign authority is exercised. When I spoke of area, I said that the borders of an area are not as clearly determined. And that in that context, area is part of an area which isn't clearly defined, it doesn't have clearly defined borders, whether they can deviate one kilometre to the left or to the right. And it was in this way that I distinguished between the two terms; namely, territory and area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Very well. I'm going to ask you to look at an exhibit, and I think the binder of exhibit is next to your desk, and it's an exhibit that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Bos. If I look at the transcript and I have heard it like this, page 20, line 7, 8, 9. I'm quoting what is written here. "When I spoke of an area, I said that the borders of an area are not as clearly determined. And that in that context, area is part of an area which isn't clearly defined ..." Now, I find this a bit strange. You say "area is part of an area." Did you mean area is part of a territory, or did you use the term "podrucje" twice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm trying to remember. I don't know if I've been precise enough, but I believe that a minute ago I explained my view of the definition of territory and area, and that it's the same that I explained on Monday. If the borders of an area are not clearly defined, you have, let's say, a surface area, space, which isn't clearly delineated with certain markers, then, of course, we can consider this area to be part of territory since territory has clearly defined borders.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Judge Trechsel, I think one of the problems of the confusion is that the interpreters, you know, may not know exactly how to translate, or, well, they may know but which may be different from what Mr. Perkovic thinks on how to interpret this term into English.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Let's move on to 1D 02011 which is a Defence exhibit that was shown to you also on Thursday [sic]. You'll find the number on the tabs, Mr. Perkovic. It's 1D 02011. Maybe the usher can help you.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please enlarge this?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: It's the fourth document from that one. Now, you were shown this document yesterday as well. It's a report; and if we look at the last page of the report, it bears your signature on page 6. And it's a list of the various decrees that I think your commission reviewed before they were adopted. Is that correct? This is in the period January to June 1993.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: If we look on this -- have a closer look on this list and then particularly on the original B/C/S version of this list, and if we look at the titles, you will see that the terms "teritorija" and "podrucje" are really being used interchangeable, I would say. For example, just listing the ones where the reference is made to "te ritorija," number 2, number 10, number 11, number 13, number 18, number 25, number 27, number 30, number 39, number 40, number 43, number 49, and number 50. And in all those laws, there's a reference to the term "teritorija," and then in other laws, again, there's a reference to the term "podrucje." Now, is it correct that the decrees on this list were all reviewed by the Commission of Regulation of which you were the head of?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my response -- or rather, let me first answer your question. I think that under our procedure the regulations commission was duty-bound to advance an opinion on each and every draft decree, which I believe it did. I can't say that it was done in every case but in most of the cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Very well. And -- but given your evidence this week about the distinction between "teritorija" and podrucje," wouldn't you agree that if we look at this list that according to your theory, all these decrees should have had the term "podrucje" and that every decree where it says "teritorija" is basically a wrong term in the title of the decree? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried to explain this yesterday when I said that in the procedure of passing decrees in that period up until the time when the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna was constituted, we had only one filter in place; whereas, in the republic, there were six or seven such filters. So such omissions are possible. Unfortunately, these are not the only omissions that there are. As I read those decrees and regulations, I saw that there were many technical omissions that should have been prevented. But given that there were only three of us working there and that two of my colleagues had never done any work in administration, it was only to be expected that there would be omissions on the part of this commission, and we see that this was indeed the case. And I think that the use of the word "territory" is contrary to the fundamental decisions of the HZ HB which all contain the term "area," "podrucje," and I think that this was an omission on the part of the commission. In other words, I was responsible because I was the head of the commission. I was responsible for the omissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Very well. I'd like you to look at another document which is Exhibit P 00019.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I just dwell --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: -- for a moment on this which has always arose my interest. You have admitted that your commission committed an omission, but there was someone else who first drafted this who also seems to have mixed up the terms, so there's already two now; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you look at those decrees, Your Honour, you will see that for the most part they come from the so-called economic departments, departments where there were no lawyers working. When we talked about those terms yesterday and the day before yesterday, I said that in everyday parlance many people, intellectuals, people with come education, but people who are not legal professionals use those two terms as synonymous, interchangeably. So I can't rule out the possibility that when these decrees were being drafted in various departments, this term might have been used by people who saw the two as being identical because they never thought about the legal use of these terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Were these decrees not ultimately adopted by someone else than your commission? Your commission didn't formally adopt them, did it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The regulations commission merely provided its opinion about the draft decrees; and when I now admitted that there was an omission on the part of the commission, I assume that in the opinions that we provided regarding the decrees when -- where there was this mistake that this was not pointed out, the fact that an improper term was used there. And as we analysed the regulations of the HZ HB, we saw that those decrees were tabled before the HVO of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and that the HVO of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna adopted these legal instruments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: So that was the third opportunity to take note of this incorrect, as you admit, incorrect terminology; and at the HVO, I suppose there were some lawyers around and wouldn't they at least have read the title?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Between the institution proposing a regulation and the institution adopting the regulation, there was only the commission, and it is not an incident that such a complicated procedure was in place in the republic for passing or adopting regulations. We were aware of it, but unfortunately we did not have the resources in terms of personnel, finances, and so on, to set up such a control mechanism. That is why I say that such omissions on the part of the commission were quite likely, and most of the members of the government were not lawyers and they did not really have to know all that. And this is the case even today. Members of the government do not have to be aware of all the legal nuances in the meaning of some terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Bos, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Trechsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, can I ask you to have a look at another exhibit which is P 00019; it's probably all the way in the front of the binder. Now, this document, while you're trying to find it, is the Constitution of Croatia, and the original version in B/C/S is the one that was published in the Narodne Novine and the English translation of it was an English translation from the Croatian government -- from the Croatian parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Before any questions are asked, may we ask for relevance of this particular document being shown to the gentleman and why. As I understand it, the gentleman has not worked for the Republic of Croatia. That testimony hasn't come in on cross -- on direct examination. So if we could have at least some sort of guidance as to why this document is being shown, unless it's for comparative purposes, in which case perhaps we should bring in the Constitution of Hungary, Slovenia, Poland, some other countries as well. I don't know. What is the relevance of this?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: The relevance is, again, on the term "teritorija" and "podrucje" and how this term is being used in the Croatian Constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In that event, I definitely object. We're talking about apples and pears. One, we're talking about the Republic of Croatian which is a country. Here, we are talking about a community which was provided for in the Constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So, with that respect, I do object to this line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to the Chamber, we have an issue with the terms of "teritorija" and "podrucje." The Prosecutor is trying to clarify this with the witness, and in doing so he submits a document from the Croatian parliament. And I suppose that on the basis of that text, the Prosecutor is going to ask the witness if the terms used in that particular document are terms that are generally used in law. This is your purpose, Mr. Bos, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, yes, and the Croatian constitution is written in exactly the same language as the laws that Mr. Perkovic drafted. And this is purely a language issue, so I really do not see why we cannot use this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Here's what's happening. I understand that the Prosecution's theory is the Croatian Community is a state within a state. We even heard members from the Trial Chamber at occasion heard that it was a state or a para-state. We object to that. Now we're trying to say here's a constitution of a country, and we're going to use their terms where they're describing their territory of a country recognised by the UN versus a community where it never asked the UN for any recognition. And it had specific reasons, it was temporary in nature, it's very clear, and I don't think it's appropriate. That's why. Now, if they can show somewhere in the constitution that they're referring to an area within Croatia and the word "territory" used for that area, that's one thing, but this is what I object to. And I understand that we have a goal in mind and we're going to try to reach that goal, and I understand what's happening over here, that they want to give the Trial Chamber the ability to tick off the boxes. I'm saying: No. This is not an appropriate method. Now, I would like to hear from the Bench how this comparison can be made.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Purely a language issue, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber dismisses the objection. It is in the transcript, it may be used later on by Mr. Prlic's Defence if they so wish, but it is the opinion of the Chamber that you should carry on. So please, Mr. Bos.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Mr. Perkovic, can I draw your attention to Article 2 of the constitution, and let me read out the third paragraph of this article: "The Republic of Croatia so exercise in accordance with international law sovereign rights and jurisdiction in the maritime areas and the seabed and subsoil thereof of the Adriatic Sea outside the state territory up to the borders with its neighbours." Now, Mr. Perkovic, if we look at the B/C/S version of this particular part of Article 2, is it correct that it's referring to the term "podrucje"?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may ask you to show Article 3 in the Croatian language, if I can see it on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, you will have a hard copy in the binder, Mr. Perkovic. We can have it on the screen, but on the back of the English version is the B/C/S version. I'm sorry. We've organized it the other way around, so first the English version and then the B/C/S. It's Article 2 and then the third paragraph. Do you have it in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, this is fully consistent with what I have said. In Article 3, there is mention of the exercise of the jurisdiction of the Republic of Croatia outside of the state area, "podrucje"; and in this article, the term "podrucje" is properly used --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat this answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Mr. Perkovic, Mr. Perkovic, the interpreters didn't catch you, so I'm afraid you will have to repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The example that you showed, paragraph 3 in Article 2, is fully consistent with what I have said. In paragraph 3, it is stated that the Republic of Croatia shall exercise its jurisdiction in maritime areas, "podrucje," and in the area of the Adriatic Sea outside of the state area, "podrucje," up until the borders with its neighbours. So the term "podrucje," area, is used here to define a coastal area outside of the territory of the Republic of Croatia in the sense of this definition, because this area in the coastal area is not strictly defined in terms of its borders as is the border of the Republic of Croatia. And I think that this example is fully consistent with what I have said in my explanation. And just one more note, I think that it would be quite interesting to look at - I'm sorry that you don't have it - if we're talking about legal terminology that is in use in Bosnia-Herzegovina and in the Croatian language and all the regulations are published in that language, you should have shown us the constitutions of the cantons, including the Croat cantons, so that we could see what terminology is used when the borders of those cantons are being defined.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Perkovic, thank you for your answer, but I'm going to disagree with you on this one. When we read this article, and particularly the last part of the third paragraph, it says: "... the subsoil territory of the Adriatic Sea outside the state territory up to the borders with its neighbours." Now, as far as I am concerned, the state territory here means the complete territory of Croatia, and not just parts of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm going to object. The counsel now is testifying. We can -- you know, he can put that in his closing argument, but this is an improper form of the question. If he wishes to put it in the form of a question, that's different. I saw no inflection, rather than this was a declarative statement, and I took that to be a closing statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bos, you made a statement. You could have asked a question. You could have said: If I tell you that, do you agree or disagree? And he may have answered you: I disagree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in light of the objection raised by my learned friend Mr. Karnavas, I didn't want to interrupt earlier. But at page 26 at line 14 to 17, there we have a question of my learned friend Mr. Bos, where he says that the Croatian constitution uses the same language as the laws that Mr. Perkovic drafted. It's again the counsel testifying. He's simply testifying here -- [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is a fact that needs to be proven.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I was referring to the Croatian language --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may, just to draw your attention to the translation of this provision in paragraph 3 of Article 2 of the Constitution of the Republic of Croatia, I would like to stress that in the Croatian text, the term that is used is "drzavnoga podrucje," "state area." And in the English version, this has been translated as "state territory." So, again, we have a situation where the term "podrucje" is translated into English as "territory."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had not failed to notice this. Mr. Bos.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise for taking up the time, but only one line of my objection is now on the transcript. It appears that my microphone had gone off although the light was on. So, for the record, let me repeat that my learned friend Mr. Prosecutor, I didn't want to interrupt him earlier, but my learned friend at page 26, lines 14 through 17, we have his question recorded as follows: He claims that the Croatian constitution is written in a completely -- in the same language as the laws that Mr. Perkovic drafted. And I claim that this is counsel testifying about facts, because the question whether the Croatian language as used in the Croatian constitution is completely identical with the language that was in use in Bosnia and Herzegovina in the Croatian language in 1993/1994, it's a fact that has to be established. This is testimony; it's not a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, Witness, you speak the language which in this Tribunal is called B/C/S. According to you, when you drafted a text for Herceg-Bosna at the time, if you compare the language you used then and the language which is used in the Croatian constitution, is it the same language or is it a different -- or are there differences?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I always say that I speak the Croatian language as an ethnic Croat. And the language that Croats speak in Bosnia and Herzegovina is called the Croatian language by us; although, to a certain extent, this language is different from the Croatian language used by most of the people in the Republic of Croatia. Linguistically speaking, let me give you an example. I know, for instance, that in the Republic of Croatia, the term "pismohrama" is used for what we call "arhiva," "archive." In Bosnia and Herzegovina, as I said, we use the term "arhiva" for "archive," and we feel that "arhiva" is also a Croatian word that is part of the Croatian language. There are other differences. But when the decrees of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna were being drafted, we tried to draft them in the Croatian language in accordance with our usage and the usage of our parents, fathers, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Final question: Imagine you would have had to draft the Constitution of the Republic of Croatia, it's just a hypothesis, would you have used the exact terms which are now used in the Constitution of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would have used the Croatian language in the same way that I use it when I write today. And to give you a striking example, in the place where I was born that we discussed at length yesterday, in Livno, at the main square there is a monument to the Croatian King Tomislav. And when this monument was being restored five years ago, the term "hiladujgodisnjica" was used instead of "tisucgodisnjica" for a "thousand." And Croats from that area put that in because, they thought and they felt that "hiladujgodisnjica" is a word that we have been using for centuries in Bosnia and Herzegovina for the number of 1.000, and we thought that this was part of the Croatian language. And I have yet to see a single piece of legislation or regulation in the Republic of Croatia that uses the term "hiladujgodisnjica." They only use the term "tisucgodisnjica." So there is a difference in the way in which you look at things. I'm sorry. I forgot to switch off my mobile phone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So there is a difference, not a big difference, but there is a difference also in legal terminology that is in use in the Croatian language in Bosnia-Herzegovina, as opposed to the legal terminology that is used in the Croatian language in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Tomasegovic Tomic. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Unlike the previous people who spoke here in courtroom, I would like to say that I think that the witness does not have the requisite expertise to provide an answer to the question why the term "podrucje" was used in Article 2 instead of the term "teritorija." This is a term that has to do with the international law of the sea. I'm not an expert so I couldn't -- and I also can't testify here and I couldn't provide you with a correct answer. But I do remember that this was at issue at the time that the term "podrucje" was used advisedly in light of the provisions of the international law of the sea, and an expert for this area of the law could provide you an answer. Also, it would perhaps be wise to look at Articles 32 and 33 to assist us because again the term "teritorija" is used, and this is an article that all of us would be able to understand better given our legal background, including the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let's proceed, Mr. Bos, because personally I want this to be on record. I do think that this is not a very important issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And I was about to move away from the issue. I can see that Mr. Praljak was on his feet and I see also that it's almost 10.30, so maybe Mr. Praljak can say something or we can maybe have the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, I know that you've already taken the floor on linguistic issues and semantic issues. The floor is yours. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. You have heard my colleague explain this. You can say or you can use the term "area" to describe somebody's occupation. You can say he is working in the area of mathematics, law, or medicine. I don't want to waste your time, but these are two completely terms, and the context of the terms are based on the usage in any given language. And this is the only way in which we can get at the sense and the contents of a term.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's 10.30. We're going to have a break because it's time, and we'll resume in 20 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. The court is back in session. Mr. Bos.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Mr. Perkovic, I would like you to look at another document, which is P 00302, and this document is the founding document of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, the 18 November 1991 founding document. You have the document in front of you? I would like to focus your attention to --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: -- to Article 2 of this document, which reads: "The Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna shall consist of the following municipalities ..." and then we have a whole list of names of municipalities. Now, what we see here is there are two municipalities, and one of them is Skender Vakuf where between brackets there is another name, Dobratici - sorry for the pronunciation - and the other one is the last one, Trebinje, and then in brackets Ravno. Now, is it correct, Mr. Perkovic, that Dobratici and Ravno were actually areas in Skender Vakuf and Trebinje?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These are parts of the municipality of Ravno and the municipality of Skender Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So you're saying parts of the municipality of Ravno or the municipality of Trebinje?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ravno is part of the Trebinje municipality, and Dobratici is part of the Skender Vakuf municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Very well. Now, Mr. Perkovic, doesn't it imply that if specific areas are being mentioned here as being part of the Croatian community, that for the other municipalities, the full territory would be part of the Croatian community?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're talking about an original document from the 18th of November, 1991, where the community established in part of an area where this -- these people live, and the areas of Dobratici and Ravno gravitate in organizational terms towards this community. However, if we look at the time-period and if we look at Article 2, then we'll see that an enormous part of the areas inhabited by the Croats, which is the subject otherwise of this document, is not regulated by this particular decree, such as Posavina -- Bosnian Posavina and other large areas such as Zepce. So this is an 18th of November document where Dobratici and Ravno were set up as separate organizational units of the party, of the political party. As I said at the start of my answer, at that point in time - and this was confirmed by the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina - this particular aspect of organizing was viewed as organizing along the political party line.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: You didn't really answer my question, but maybe I can phrase it differently. According to you, the municipalities, other than Skender and Trebinje, would this particular decision have meant the complete territory of the municipalities or parts of these territory?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat, the emphasis was on the political party organizing. There was the basic structure of the HDZ in Ravno and basic structure of the HDZ in Dobratici. Since these two organizations were present in the area, that's the reason why --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Mr. Perkovic, Mr. Bos now has started off by saying, "You have not really answered my question," and I think he has a strong point. Now, you should not repeat what you have said before, but you should actually answer his question because you make us lose a lot of time otherwise.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, we're talking about the organizing in parts of the territory of the municipality or the area of Skender Vakuf and the area of Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, maybe I have not been clear, and I will again repeat the question. My question concerns the other municipalities listed in the article, not Skender Vakuf and Trebinje. In your opinion, did the drafters of this decision intend to include the full territory of the municipalities as part of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as this decision is concerned, the entire territory of these municipalities was included in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna in terms of the political party organizing because there were municipal party structures based in individual municipalities, and the areas they covered as political party structures were identical to the areas of municipalities themselves. And I was referring to HDZ structures.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So, well, I'm trying to understand your question [sic]. So can we take it from your question [sic] that you're saying that the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna at that time was the entire territory of the municipalities listed in Article 2?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, save for the municipalities of Trebinje and Skender Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Very well. Very well. Okay. I think we can skip the following exhibit, and then I would like to move to another topic which is the constitutional legitimacy of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. And I would like you for that to refer to document 2D 00594, and this is a document that you were shown also I think on Monday. It's all the way in the back, Mr. Perkovic. Do you have the document?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Do you recall this document from Monday?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to focus your attention under item 2, and in particular the second paragraph, and maybe I'll just read it out to you: "Based on mentioned opinions, as well as propositions and opinions which were voiced during the discussion, the Government determined that Decision on implementation of Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and Decision by Regional committee of HDZ Bosnian Posavina were not reached according to procedure specified for creation of social political communities, neither they contain regulations which could produce any kind of legal effects such as implementation of the institutions of the authority because they lack elements of the government institutions." Now, would you agree with me with what's been said here is that the BH government, you know, may have not found that the HDZ wasn't illegal -- the HZ HB was an illegal organization, but, nevertheless, that they could not be considered government institution because they lacked elements for that purpose? Is that how I should understand this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The government finds in this paragraph that you've quoted that the HZ HB has not been established and does not operate as a socio-political association, community. Under the then-system, the levels of the municipality, town, and republic were considered to be socio-political communities. The government of the HB --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: BH.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- believed that the HZ HB did not fall into this category of being a socio-political community and that the decision it adopted does not show any intentions of it exerting authority as a state has authority. And in line with this, the government goes on to conclude that on the basis of this, there is no need for the government to discuss this at one of its meetings. This is something that I said, that the government did not consider this to be any sort of state authority in view of who the founders of that structure were, and in view of the fact that the HZ HB as -- or rather, that the HDZ BH as a legitimately established political party in the BH was entitled to use whatever forms of political party organizing it sees fit to use. On the basis of this, the government found that there was -- there were no grounds for the procedure of the assessment of the constitutionality of this decision to be instituted.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: It's exactly on that last point that I wanted to come back to, because it's correct that you drafted an opinion on this issue which I think is the opinions that have been referred to here in this document. And in your opinion, you included that the BH government in relation to the legality of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, that this community was not an illegal form of organization and that there was no basis for a complaint to be filed before the constitutional court. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I participated in the development of the draft of this opinion, as I said, together with another colleague of mine. Under the constitution of Bosnia -- or rather, when this opinion was forwarded to a government meeting, under the Constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the government ex officio, once it finds that the constitution has been violated, is duty-bound to initiate the relevant procedure before the constitutional court. Given the fact that the government has not taken any steps after having considered this decision, it is only logical to conclude that the establishment of the Croatian Community HB at the time in November 1992 -- or rather, sorry, 1991 was not considered to be anti-constitutional.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, we've just saw the founding document of the Croatian community was adopted on the 18th of November; and so this document, as you say -- this meeting in the BH government was held on the 21st of November. So I presume in that period, between 18 November and the 21st, that in those two days, you and your colleagues actually drafted this opinion on the basis of the document -- the founding document that we just saw before; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, I would like you to look at Exhibit P 00476, and this is, in fact, the constitutional court decision which was published on the 18th of September, 1992. P 00476, it's again somewhere in the beginning of the binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Maybe the usher can assist to get the document in the binder, P 00476.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you first, have you ever seen this decision of the constitutional court?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, once, but I believe it was after the war in 1996 or 1997 that I had the occasion of reading it for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, it's dated 18 September 1992. At that time, you were in Sarajevo, weren't you? You returned to Sarajevo in August 1992 and you left again in December 1992. So when this decision was published, you never noticed that? You were in Sarajevo. Was this something that just simply didn't get your attention?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Upon my return to Sarajevo, immediately as I got there, I learned that another individual had been appointed to my position. I requested that I be given an opportunity to return to my post. I said that I had practically no business to discharge in Sarajevo for two months, save for arranging the regulations that were relevant. So, given that I was outside of these institutions, I was unable to access such information. If you're not receiving Official Gazettes, then I don't think you're able to get informed since at the time the newspaper stands were closed. And I believe all those who were present in Sarajevo at the time can vouch for the fact that I would not have been able to get by this information unless I had been part of the government institutions. It is for this reason that I saw this decision only after the war, since I was interested in the statement of reasons laid out in that decision of the constitutional court.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Very well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for His Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You have described your activity as, I quote from page 41, line 7, " ... arranging the regulations that were relevant." I must confess that I cannot understand what this refers to. Can you explain more precisely what you did.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, Your Honour, I do not understand your question. Are you asking me what it was that I was doing in Sarajevo in terms of organizing regulations, what I was just referring to or something else?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: No, that's right. I quote again what you are written down here as having said. I quote from the end of line 5, page 41: "I said that I had practically no business to discharge in Sarajevo for two months, save for arranging the regulations that were relevant." It's this last half sentence that I would be grateful if you could explain what it means.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Upon my arrival in Sarajevo, I spent the first 15 days trying to arrange with my colleagues amendments to the regulations then valid in the BH which had to do with the organization of the judiciary in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Since I did not accept the position that was offered to me, which was at a much lower level, and in view of the fact that over these 15 days I didn't have any other engagements because it was impossible to leave Sarajevo, I was left practically without any duties at all for the subsequent two months, and I was hoping that I would be able to find a way to leave Sarajevo. As a result of that, for these two months, I was neither in the Ministry of the Administration nor was I doing anything else, except for trying to find a way to get out of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Perkovic, let's have a closer look at this decision, and particularly the first part of the decision. Now, what we see here is a -- it starts offer with a whole list of decrees from the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. There's nine in total. And then there's the statement of reasons which starts by saying: "On July 1992 on its own initiative, the constitutional court initiated proceedings for the evaluation of the legality and constitutionality of the above-mentioned general enactments." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, would you agree with me that decision is based on nine enactments of which one of them was the decision on the establishment of the Croatian community of 18 November, the first one; whereas, you would have based your opinion on the first document only, wouldn't you agree that the constitutional court did not only evaluate this one decision but, in fact, nine subsequent -- eight subsequent decisions of the Herceg-Bosna community? So, in fact, the constitutional court evaluated this at a time that Herceg-Bosna was much more developed than at the time that you rendered your opinion? Would you agree or know that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're discussing the period of time of just under one year after the establishment of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. In that period of time, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna evolved as it did; and for that reason, the quality of the relations within the HZ HB at the time when it was being examined by the constitutional court following the 18th of November -- on the 18th of November and in the subsequent period differed greatly. When we were discussing the areas covered and the organization of the structure, well, that was a rather different situation that we had in September 1992 compared to the situation when the founding enactment was adopted. At that period, in 1992, the HZ HB had taken upon itself the role of defending the Croat people in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Perkovic. I think we're going to leave this document aside now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please. To your knowledge, Witness, the constitutional court at the time and still today, was it in a position to examine such cases of its own accord, or was it necessary for the government or political party to seize the constitutional court? Based on the legislation at the time, were the judges of the constitutional court allowed to act of their own accord?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The procedure of the evaluation of constitutionality before the constitutional court, as far as I can remember the provisions of the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina, could be initiated by the highest authorities in the country; namely, the parliament, the Assembly, that is, of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Most often, the procedure was initiated pursuant to a proposal or the initiative of the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina. When it comes to this particular decision, I wish to note that a number of important provisions which concern the mechanism according to which decisions are rendered by the constitutional court were not honoured, primarily the entitlement of the party proposing or adopting a given enactment to give its opinion before the constitutional court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The constitutional court was in a position to give its evaluation after having decided to examine the matter proprio motu; that's my question. Was that possible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Under the Constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina, it was possible. I believe that the constitutional court could initiate the procedure proprio motu and render a decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Mr. Perkovic, I now want to move again to August 1992, and I want to read out again a part of your testimony from the Kordic case and see if it jogs your memory. This is page number 20587 of the testimony of 7 June 2000 in the Kordic case, and I'll read out the parts which I'm interested in: "When the war began in Bosnia-Herzegovina, relevant contacts with representatives of financial institutions were maintained so that in August 1992 at Siroki Brijeg, that is, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna directly, the prime minister of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mr. Jure Pelivan, and the minister of finance of the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mr. Mustafa or Mahmut Logo, I'm not sure, came to that Siroki Brijeg. "At that meeting held at Siroki Brijeg the discussion, the discussion also broached the subject of the issue of Bosnian legal tender, and those gentlemen showed a specimen of what that future currency of Bosnia-Herzegovina should look like." Do you recall this evidence, Mr. Perkovic, and do you recall that meeting?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember the meeting with Mr. Pelivan and Mr. Logo. The meeting was held in Siroki Brijeg and was attended by the Croatian officials from various institutions of Bosnia-Herzegovina who happened to be in the area. I do recall that a number of issues were discussed including Mr. Pelivan, prime minister of the HZ HB, showing us the prototype of a BH bank note and telling us that very soon that legal tender would be placed in circulation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Do you recall who from the Croatian Herzegovina community were present at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can recall some people who held appropriate posts in the organs of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.
