I think that it was Mr. Bozo Misura, who was head of the general services of the organs of the republic; Mr. Miroslav Palameta, who was the deputy minister of education of Bosnia and Herzegovina; I think that there was also Mr. Mariofil Ljubic, who was the deputy president of the BH parliament; and there were some other people. I can't recall all of them, but I know that there was a certain number of people there at that meeting, people who held appropriate positions in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And when Mr. Pelivan came with this specimen of a new BH currency and came with that proposal to introduce this currency, what was the reaction of the Herceg-Bosna authorities who were present at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this meeting, the meeting that we're talking about, Mr. Pelivan just outlined briefly the activities that he and the people in the Government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina were engaged in; and in the context of this short briefing that he gave us, he showed us this specimen and he said what I've just told you, that preparations were underway to circulate BH currency. The focus of the discussion was on reaching an agreement about the return of the Croatian personnel to their jobs in Sarajevo or an alternative solution proposed by Mr. Pelivan as the prime minister, which was that part of the state administration be relocated from Sarajevo to Zenica. We all participated in the debate about this proposal, and we supported it because we knew that it would be much simpler to do this work in Zenica than in Sarajevo; on the other hand, we understood that because of the overall situation in Sarajevo, it was impossible for the entire administration to simply move because that would mean that they would leave the capital in the lurch. But we thought that there could be a good compromise for just some elements of the administration to leave and to start working in Zenica. All of us who worked in the organs of the republic at the time told Mr. Pelivan that we were prepared to resume our posts and to continue working on our old jobs in a new location if an agreement were to be achieved to that effect. Unfortunately, ten or 15 days after that, that was on the eve of my departure to Sarajevo, I said that I had flown back into Sarajevo on the same plane as Mr. Pelivan. But on my arrival in Sarajevo, I immediately realized that there was not support of this idea that was mooted by the prime minister. So, at that meeting, there was no debate about the way in which this money were to be circulated, there was just this brief instance when the prime minister showed us the specimen. But the prime minister had a number of meetings in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I cannot rule out the possibility that this issue was discussed at one such meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Just in order to clarify what you've just said, when you say that the Bosnian Croat authorities reacted positively to the proposal, this was when you were talking about the proposal to open an office in Zenica, but I was specifically asking you about this proposal for this new BH currency. Did they -- at least that's how I understood your answer, and correct me if I'm wrong. But did that also include -- were they also positive to that proposal for the new BH currency? Can you clarify that.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you that this was a meeting with the representatives of the Croatian people that were in the organs of the republic in Sarajevo. I did not speak about the Bosnian Croat authorities. I spoke about the representatives of the Croatian people who worked in the organs of the republic in Sarajevo; they attended the meeting. And since the new BH currency was not discussed at all, I told you what was on the agenda of that meeting, and let me repeat it once again. It was the expectations raised by the prime minister that we should all go back to our jobs and his idea that a part of the administration should move out to Zenica. The entire meeting with us -- the entire meeting with us was spent discussing how best to ensure the functioning of the administration outside of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So, well, sorry that I may have misunderstood, and I'm just going to clarify and hopefully ask it one more time. So that meeting was not with members of the Croatian community, but these were all Croats from the BiH administration in Sarajevo who met in Siroki Brijeg. Is that how I should understand it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, let's move then to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Before we move on, Your Honour, I do wish to point out that the gentleman gave a more fuller explanation in his testimony during the Kordic trial. The Prosecution read approximately from lines 3 to line 16 of page 20587, but the gentleman did go on to state that for whatever reason that currency was not used, that coupons were used instead, and, of course, German marks. So I do wish to put -- so either the entire page or the entire question and answer from that section of the Kordic trial should be introduced into evidence, or at least the gentleman should be given an opportunity to comment on that or at least make sure to validate that that is exactly -- that that is the entire answer to the question being posed. And I state this because otherwise it gives the impression that you have the government of Sarajevo coming down, talking about a currency, then the Croats in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna using other currency, thereby giving the impression that the idea was pushed aside by the Croats in the Croatian community when, in fact, the Bosnian dinar never came into circulation as it had been expected. I think that is the complete story.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, following this objection, can you confirm that as part of your testimony in the Kordic case you gave the information Mr. Karnavas has just provided?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The fact is that this currency was not used even in the areas controlled by the BH army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Mr. Bos.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Mr. Perkovic, moving to another topic again. On Monday, you testified that the HVO was to be seen as a necessity or an alternative for the state institutions of Bosnia-Herzegovina that ceased to effectively function in the region of Herceg-Bosna. Do you recall that evidence?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Do you recall that the BH government around August 1992 rendered a decree to establish a district system in order to control and govern the full territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the time of war? Do you remember that the BH government rendered this -- well, came with this decree to implement districts in the Bosnia-Herzegovina area?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know that this decree was passed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Maybe you could have a look at the text of the decree, which is 1D 00509. Do you have it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please assist me and tell me where is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Somewhere in the back of the binder, 1D 00509, and the usher will assist you. Now, we see here it's dated 13 August 1992, a decree with the power of law on establishment and work of districts, and let me just read out Article 1: "By means of this Decree, Districts as special socio-political communities shall be established to function during the state of war (in further text: Districts), as well as their names, centres, and territories, their rights and duties, the organization and scope of competence of District bodies and district executive bodies and district bodies in the organization and preparation of citizens for armed fight in the territory of District, as well as and other issues of interest for the organization and work of District." Now, you've stated that you've seen this decree. Is it correct that in October 1992, there was an amendment to the decree because I think initially, if we look at Article 6, the decree was -- set up seven districts; and then, in October 1992, they reorganize this and it became ten districts. If you look at the one-but-last page of the document, you'll see the amendments to this decree. It's on --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. The decree from October 1992 amended the original text of the decree.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And if we look in this list of ten districts, we see under number 4 the district of Mostar and under number 10 the district of Livno. And would you agree that the municipalities listed for these two districts in general, maybe not fully, but covered a lot of the area which was covered under Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we're talking about the Livno district, because it's smaller so let's take that as our starting point, in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, there was no area of the municipalities of Glamoc, the municipality of Glamoc, in fact. So if we're talking about the Mostar district, practically all the municipalities in the area called Eastern Herzegovina were not part of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, the municipalities of Bileca, Gacko, Ljubinje, Nevesinje, Trebinje, with the exception of Ravno, the area of Ravno.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Very well. That's what we saw on the document. Now, Witness, would you agree with me that this decree that was rendered here by the BiH government was a serious attempt of the BiH government to sort of control and govern the full territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina while being at war?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my deep conviction that this is an unconstitutional attempt on the part of the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina because the issue of the internal organization of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the issue of the number of socio-political communities or the level of socio-political communities is provided for in the constitution of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And I think that the government passing a bylaw that has a force of a law could not change the internal structure of the government in Bosnia and Herzegovina. And let me go back to the question that was asked before the break. I think that the constitutional court of Bosnia and Herzegovina should have reacted either proprio motu or at the proposal of another institution in the same manner in which it did following the decisions enacted by the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna if it really had been its intention to protect the provisions of the Constitution of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Very well. Okay. That's -- that is your opinion. Could I ask you to look at document 1D 02565. It's another Defence exhibit, and this is a document dated the 23rd of February, 1993. And you will see that -- you will see that the document, the first two pages -- I'm sorry, you're still --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Again, maybe the usher can help. It's document 1D 02565.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: It's, again, near the end of the binder, Mr. Perkovic. If you have the document, you will see that the first two pages are letters. The first one is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation] MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't know, please interrupt me if this is not important, but I did not have the Prosecution documents before, and I have managed to read the previous document only now. That's document 1D 00509. I managed to read Articles 1 and 3 in the B/C/S version, in Croatian, and I could see that the terms "podrucje" and "teritorija" in the Croatian are rendered as "territory" in the English version. This is of particular importance in Article 1, 3, paragraph 3, because we can see that a distinction is drawn in the same manner in which it was done in the HZ HB documents we looked at earlier. Perhaps it would be best for the witness to read the text of this article -- of this document, Articles 1 and 3, in Croatian. This is an official document of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and this distinction is clearly visible. That's why I think it would be a good idea, to clarify this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm going to ask to have this done in re-direct. This is again -- you know, I would really like to continue with my evidence, and this is really a matter which should be dealt with in --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel pause for the interpreters between questions and answers, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Is there a ruling on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I know my --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I know there is a shaking by one of the Judges, but is there a ruling, because if there is an objection. I do think this shouldn't be dealt with on my time. This is something that the Court should deal with on its time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is an objection. What I meant is that during the break, I looked up the words in a Serbo-Croatian dictionary, Cambridge publisher, and this is a dictionary we use here, so please use it. And as to the translation of the word "podrucje," there are three words, territory, region, area. This is it. So the three English words are used to render "podrucje." Now, Mrs. Tomic has just told us that this was translated into English as "territory." Well, no wonder, because this is in the dictionary. What we can do is refer this to the translation service where there are competent people who will provide us with the accurate translation of this term; otherwise, we may go on about this for hours and hours. My colleague will ask the floor and say some things, Mr. Bos will say, and other counsel will say something. It's going to go on for days. We have this relevant language service, the CLSS, and they should be providing us with the answer. Now, this being said, if the Defence thinks that this is of paramount importance and that the whole trial is based on this term, you're entitled to summoning a linguistic expert who will be testifying for hours and days to talk to us about this. Now, let's proceed, Mr. Bos.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Mr. Perkovic, you have the document in front of you, I can see. Now, you'll see that the first two pages are --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: -- letters, sort of cover letters for the document, that then follows on the third page which is -- and maybe we'll just see. The first letter is sent to Mr. Demirovic; the second cover letter is sent to Mr. Pasalic, commander of the 4th Corps; and copies of that letter are sent to the CSB, Mr. Ramo Maslesa and Mr. Jadranko Prlic, as the plenipotentiary of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to focus your attention now on the documents starting on the third page, which is a document from the Government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the setting up of Mostar and Livno districts. And the Prosecution thinks this is an important document, so I'm going to read out a large part of the document so this may take a while. But I think it's important that we get this on the record, and I'll start with reading the second paragraph of that document and you can follow from the hard copy: "In accordance with the latest information" -- and this is a document dated 25th of February, 1993, and it's starting on the second paragraph: "In accordance with the latest information from the districts, obtained until February 25th, 1993, the district organs had been formed in the following districts: Bihac, Gorazde, Tuzla, and Zenica; in Banja Luka, Doboj, Sarajevo, and Travnik districts. Republic commissions were formed for these districts, and this commissions perform the function of the Presidencies of these districts."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Next page on the original, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: "Mostar district for the territories of the following municipalities," and I won't read out all of them, but then also, "and Livno district for the territories of the following municipalities ... are not in function yet." And then third paragraph, and I will read that in full: "Because of the familiar reasons that are in the first place of the political origin and that relate to the setting up of the authorities of the so-called 'Herceg-Bosna,' the constitution of Mostar and Livno districts did not begin immediately, in accordance with the positive regulations of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. "However, the Government of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, with the aim to set up these districts, sent a letter to Mr. Mate Boban on 29 September 1992, in which, when speaking of the issue of setting up of these districts, the following was said among other things: At the beginning of the war, in very complex situation in Mostar and Livno regions, the temporary organs of Herceg-Bosna were formed. The Agreement between the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, dated July 1, 1992, defines that the temporary authorities of Herceg-Bosna would be harmonized with the legislation of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Therefore, we propose with the aim of harmonization of practice of organization of war organs in the whole territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, you should instigate the proceedings of renaming of temporary organs of Herceg-Bosna for Mostar and Livno regions into the district organs of Mostar and Livno districts, in accordance with the mentioned decree. At the same time, it is requested from Mate Boban in this letter that he proposes the candidates for the most responsible functions in the organs and bodies of these districts." Sir, do you recall that around this time in February 1993 that the BH government was putting this proposal to implement these Mostar and Livno districts which hadn't been implemented yet?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time these events unfolded, I was not aware of them; however, I came to know something about these initiatives at a later date. Therefore, I can say that the initiative to establish districts was something I got to know about later but was not aware of at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So when did you get to know about and in what context, can you elaborate on that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I got to know about them perhaps a month or two after the initiative had been forwarded in the context of the information we received on matters concerning the internal organization of the BH institutions, and especially on those matters where different opinions were espoused. There was this one meeting discussing the internal organization of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and all these debates were closely linked with various peace plans that reached us, one after the other. We had information that the Bosniak side regarded this matter -- or rather, wanted this matter to be resolved through the establishment of districts, which would be the regional forms of socio-political communities, which in the view of the Croat side remained to be centralised a form of organization, or if not centralised at least insufficiently decentralised.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, if we look at the text, there is a reference to an agreement between the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina dated the 1st of July, 1992. Now, I've been trying to trace down this agreement, and I think that this agreement is, in fact, the agreement of the 21st of July, 1992. And I would like to show you that document which is P 00339, and this is the agreement on friendship and cooperation that was signed on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And maybe we can have a look at the text of that agreement, which is in the binder as well, P 00339.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Mr. Perkovic, do you recall that around the 21st of July, 1992, that this agreement was being -- well, was being signed by the republic -- by Mr. Izetbegovic and Mr. Franjo Tudjman, this agreement on friendship and cooperation?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This agreement received extensive media coverage so that practically every citizen in the area who followed the Croatian press or the Croatian TV was able to know that an agreement on friendship and cooperation had been signed between the two countries. Later on, some ten days later perhaps, I was able to read the text of the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could I focus your attention on item number 6 in the agreement, and then in particular the second part of item number 6; and, again, I'll read out this part: "Provisional civil authorities established in wartime conditions with the scope of the Croatian Defence Council will be made to conform as soon as possible with the constitutional-juridical system of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and talks pertaining to this matter will be initiated immediately in the spirit of the principles stated in Point 1 of this Agreement."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If he could be given an opportunity to look at point 1 since that's part of what he's being asked to comment on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: There you go. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And I can read out point 1 as well, if need be. Point 1: "The President of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the President of the Republic of Croatia have agreed that the future state system of Bosnia and Herzegovina will proceed from the principle of full equality of the three constituent nations: Muslims, Croats, and Serbs. The constitutional-political system of the country will be based on constituent units in the establishment of which due account will be taken of national, historical, cultural, economic, traffic, and other elements." Witness, would you agree with me that what's raised in point 6 is, in fact, exactly, you know, the point that the BiH government was making in that document in which they pressed about the setting up of the Livno and Mostar district, that, in fact, there was an agreement between Mr. Tudjman and Mr. Izetbegovic that these districts could be set up?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, there are several reasons at least why I cannot agree with this statement of yours, and I'll focus on the most important ones. With this agreement, the presidents of the two countries have agreed that the constitutional political system of the country would be based on constituent units. The powers given to the districts clearly show that the districts are not constituent units because the definition of a constituent unit dictates the way in which it is to be conformed to the constitution. Second, it is highly unusual that the issue of the definition of socio-political communities should be covered by the bodies of the defence. From the documents you've showed to me, we can see that it is a letter that the Ministry of Defence sent to the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina; although, according to the organisation and the remit of ministries, as far as I remember, this did not fall at all within the remit of the ministry of defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Even more unusual is the fact that in the second document you showed that me, the communications issue is resolved through the State Security Service. I'm particularly surprised by the fact that the documents you showed to me suggest that these documents be delivered to Mr. Prlic and Mr. Boban. As we know that by that time for several months already, pursuant to the decisions of the constitutional court which you asked me about a moment ago, the HZ HB is a non-constitutional entity. Therefore, I wouldn't see on what basis these organs would be communicating with Mr. Prlic and Mr. Boban. Would they be communicating with them only as with BH citizens since they did not have any other political roles than those in the HZ HB? At the same time, in that area there were Croat citizens who held certain republican positions and powers. In sum, it is evident from all the documents that were shown to me that there did not exist either the intention or the wish for a solution to be found about the internal system of Bosnia-Herzegovina between the Croats and Muslims on the principles of equality which would have been acceptable to both these peoples and which would have made possible an adjustment or a transformation of the organs of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna in the way suggested in the agreement signed by Messrs. Izetbegovic and Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, something caught my attention in your answer, and I would like to check if you said what you said. You said that the three constituent units require decisions to be taken by way of consensus. I heard you say this. Does that mean that decisions in Bosnia-Herzegovina required a agreement from the Serbs, Croats, and Muslims, although there might be disagreements on some issues, which would have meant that all the decision-making would have been blocked in the state? Is that what you actually meant? Every decision made by the Presidency or by the legislator required unanimity among the three constituent units, Muslims, Serbs, and Croats. Could you elaborate on this. You have touched upon it briefly in your answer and you were answering another question, but this really caught my attention because listening to you I thought if one of the constituent units disagreed, this would block the whole system. So is this what you actually meant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Presiding Judge, in my answer, I did not mention a -- any number of constituent units. I didn't mention three constituent units. I spoke of an undefined number of constituent units; there could have been five, seven, or ten of them. I spoke of the basic principle, which is that the issue of the internal system of a country, particularly a multi-ethnic country such as Bosnia-Herzegovina where constituent peoples live and a country which has its constituent units, that a consensus should be achieved; and on the basis of a consensus, the mechanism for decision-making can be defined. It is precisely such solutions that we have today in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the level of the state and sometimes they require that the procedures be quite lengthy, but they espouse the basic principle on which today's Bosnia-Herzegovina rests, which is the equality of the constituent peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina. From the way these districts were formulated and the way they were supposed to be established and the numbers in which they were supposed to be established as well as the powers which they were supposed to have, we could see that the decision on this had already been taken. The Croat side was practically only asked to accept what has already been defined without giving any suggestions on the issues. And the carrot given to them was that Mr. Boban or Mr. Prlic, as far as I remember, would be allowed to offer their own cadres who would be ethnic Croats to govern these districts. This approach is quite contrary to the intentions and the spirit in which the Izetbegovic-Tudjman agreement on friendship was signed. It is particularly contrary to Article 1 which we've just been referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for this accurate and exhaustive answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: In relation to this topic, let me show you one more document which is 1D 01972. It is a Defence exhibit which again will be probably in the back of your binder. Do you have the letter? It's not dated, but it starts off -- it's a letter signed by Mr. Prlic and addressed to Mr. Zlatko Lagumdzija, the vice-president of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It begins by saying: "In your letter without number of 3 March 1993, you informed me of the conclusions of the Government of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina regarding the foundation and putting into operation of the Mostar and Livno districts." Would you agree with me that this letter by Mr. Prlic is an effective response to the documents that we just saw before?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The letter is not dated. We can't see when it was sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: No, we can't, but --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But one could infer that this might be a reply to the document sent earlier. Although, in those documents that were sent earlier, I did not observe that it was Mr. Lagumdzija, the prime minister, who sent the letter to Mr. Prlic. I believe that it was a third party that was asked to send the letter to Mr. Prlic. Nevertheless, one could assume that this was an answer to or a response to those documents. I apologise, but I also observe the absence of any signatures, and this begs the question of whether this is an actual document. Mr. Prosecutor, there is no date, no signature, we only have the heading, which makes it very difficult for me to say whether this is, indeed, a letter by Mr. Prlic and whether it was ever sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Perkovic, this is a Defence exhibit, so I think we could presume that if the Defence submitted this evidence that this letter is, in fact, an authenticated letter. But looking at the content of the letter, would you agree with the position -- with the response Mr. Prlic is making in this letter?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Labouring under the assumption that this letter was sent, Mr. Prlic deals with one aspect of the problem which seems very important to me and which is the gist of what I was discussing a moment ago. That's item 4 of the letter which says that: "The establishment of the Mostar and Livno districts has not been prescribed in the Constitution of the HZ HB [as interpreted] or other enactments signed during peace negotiations by both Muslim and Croat delegations in Geneva and New York." The constitution of the BH was definitely not signed either in Geneva or in New York, so I suppose they're referring to other documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, on page 64, line 12, the gentleman said the Constitution of "BiH," as opposed to "HZ HB." Line 12, you will see. We all know that HZ HB did not have a constitution.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter corrects herself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Just one last question on this letter, Mr. Perkovic: How do you think that a letter like this would have reached Sarajevo --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: -- it must have been around March 1993 that this letter was being sent to Mr. Lagumdzija.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were several ways. It could be sent through international representatives, representatives of UNPROFOR who enjoyed at least some freedom of movement throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina. It could have been handed over to the Embassy of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Zagreb, for instance, or to some other BH embassy in the world. It could have been delivered to one of the officials of the republican organs who happened to be in the area. Just as Mr. Lagumdzija or Mr. Demirovic used to send some other documents to their own officials in the area with the request that the documents be forwarded to Mr. Boban. In other words, some sort of a roundabout mechanism could be used to make sure that a letter reached Sarajevo or reached Mostar from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Unless the Chamber has any other questions on this topic, I would like to move to another topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't have questions, but this might be a right time for the break, the last break for this morning. So we'll have a break and I'll ask the registrar to count the time during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Mr. Bos, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, I'd like you to have a look at another document in the binder probably near the end it's 1D 02018, and this is a 3 July 1992 decree on public enterprises in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. Let me read out Article 1 here: "In the interest of socio-economic development and the protection of nature and natural resources of the Croatian people and other peoples in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, the Presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna has adopted a decree establishing public enterprises in the following areas of activity," and then we see a whole list of activities: "Production, transmission, and distribution of electrical energy... water management ... forestry ... mining ... postal, telephone, and telegraph services ... rail transport ... road transport ... official journal of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna ... information activities, radio, and television ... and special purposes industry." Just on that point, (j), special purposes industry, what kind of industry would I have to think about here?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: You will have to switch on your microphone.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The special purposes industry mainly comprises military industry, the manufacture of arms and all sorts of equipment important and relevant for the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, it says here in the first line that they adopt a decree in establishing these public enterprises. Now, would that mean that these enterprises were established, or does it, in fact, mean that these enterprises already existed and were taken over? How should I read the term "establishing" here?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The other term synonymous of "utemeljiti," "establish," is "osnovati," "to found." In other words, this decree with its contents prescribes the areas in which these public companies are to be established. What follows from there is the obligation to prepare the founding documents of these public companies which are to be deposited or filed with Registry of the relevant court.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So would that mean that these enterprises did already exist or did not exist at all? Let's say, for example, let's take water management activities, any enterprises that wouldn't be established, would that be a completely new enterprise, or would that be a enterprise that already existed and then would be taken over by the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This means that a new company is being set up as a new legal entity which is registered at such with the court registry; so, in other words, it is a new public company that is being set up.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: You're saying a legal entity, but does that mean that -- maybe I can describe it -- let's phrase it this way: Would that mean that the whole company didn't exist yet, that there is still -- that there weren't any employees, that there wasn't any building, whatever, and that everything had to start from scratch, or are you talking simply legally, that they were taken over legally or established legally?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the valid regulations in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina which had been taken over and applied in this period, all the socio-political communities and authorities could establish public companies. There were municipalities which were able to establish public companies all the way up to the republican level. Here, we have the authorities of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna passing regulations which create the legal prerequisite allowing these bodies to establish no public companies as legal entities. In other words, the establishment of these companies as new legal entities did not make the existence of existing public companies null and void. Let's take as an example the power supply company. If the company of Elektroprivreda, power supply company, of Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna was set up, this did not preclude the existence of the Bosnian power supply company. What was being set up here was a new legal entity.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Is it your evidence, then, on all these items that are listed in item 1 that the Croatian communities created new entities aside from the existing BH enterprises on all these -- you know, on all these things like energy, electricity, water, postal, so is it your evidence that the BiH enterprises of these public utilities still existed and that the Croatian community simply established aside from those existing public utility companies new companies; is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And that's on all these matters that are listed?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The decree creates a possibility for public companies to be established in all these fields or branchs. Some were, in fact, set up quite soon thereafter; whereas, for some other fields, I don't know that they ever set up a public company. For instance, I know that the public company of Elektroprivreda, power supply company, of HZ HB was set up. But I don't know that in the mining industry the possibility of a public company being set up had ever been used. I don't know that a public company was ever set up in the mining industry or in the field of information. To my knowledge, the HZ HB TV was never set up and never made operational, unlike the HZ HB radio. However, that said, in most of these branchs public companies were set up.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, I won't push this point any further, but maybe then I'm going to ask you to look at another exhibit which is 1D 00196. This is an exhibit dated January 1993, and it concerns regulations on the registration of vehicles of the internal affairs department of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. Now, I'd like to focus your attention on Article 3, and let me read out this article: "Under the terms of these regulations, police markings shall be the following: A combination of colour blue number 5013 and colour white number 9010 in accordance with the RAL catalogue of colours for vehicle registration; a plate with police written on it; police number plates; and a drawing (emblem) or a police badge sticker ..." Then I'll stop there. "The plate with police written on it, the number plates, and the police badge image must be made in such a way as to reflect light." Then if I then can show you Article 13, which again describes: "The form and size of digits and letters on police number plates and plates with police written on them shall be identical to the size, colour, and form of the number plates prescribed by the regulations on vehicle registration, except that the letters and digits shall be blue. "The registration markings shall be written in the left or upper part of the number plates and shall consist of three digits, while the vehicle registration number also consisting of three digits, shall be written in the right or lower part of the number plates. In between shall be the coat of arms of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, which shall be the same size, colour, and form as the civilian number plates." Then, well, you can read the rest yourself. Now, would you agree with me that these are very detailed regulations on how the signs of a police car needs to be, you know, on the markings of a police vehicle in Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, these regulations provide for the entire appearance of registration plate, of a license plate. That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: You've testified that legislation during this period was all temporary legislation needed in order to -- you know, for wartime and for a time of war. Can you explain why a regulation like this needed to be put in place? It seems to me that you can hardly consider this as something which is really important and that, therefore, a temporary regulation needs to be established. Can you just explain, what is the importance -- I would assume that in January 1993 police vehicles were -- the existing police vehicles were well known and recognised by the people living in Herzegovina. Why was there a need, first, to change it; and, secondly, why was there a need to regulate all this?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me respond to your question backwards. The issue of regulating in detail, every public document and registration or licence plates are a kind of a public document is traditionally dealt with in this matter. When you stipulate the way in which a birth certificate should look, the format of a birth certificate or a citizenship certificate, every segment of this document is stipulated in greatest detail. Let us say that this is part of a tradition in the drafting of the regulations that pertain to the way in which public documents are to be produced or, let's say, other documents that make it possible for somebody or something to be identified. In this case, we're talking about the identification of a passenger vehicle. Going back to the second part of your question, why this had to be done, this had to be done for a very simple reason because the republican regulation that was in force until the war broke out in Bosnia and Herzegovina stipulated that police vehicles, the registration plates of the police vehicles, should bear the sign of a five-point star, a symbol of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina or the symbol of the former SFRY. So the very same symbol, sign, that caused the organs of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna to be set up in order to mount a defence against those who bore this symbol, the five-point star, on their caps as they mounted this aggression against this area. So wouldn't it seem logical to you that institutions and bodies of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna should change this symbol? And in this context, when the insignia were changed, the symbols and signs were changed, and this went for all of Bosnia and Herzegovina, including the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In Sarajevo, the coat of arms was changed. It was quite logical for those symbols and signs to be changed because the population did not want to accept those symbols, not only on the police vehicles but in other aspects of life. So this is why this was changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So if I understand what you're saying, then, for the Muslim population living in the region of Herceg-Bosna, they would agree that these symbols on the police vehicles were to be changed into symbols from the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No referendum was organized on this issue, so I cannot speak in general whether the Bosniak population agreed with that or not. But I do not know of any case in which a Bosniak or other non-Croat would protest or anything else or ask either during the war or afterwards not to drive a vehicle bearing those symbols. Perhaps one could say that during the war the people were too afraid to protest, but the same symbols were in use for almost two years after the war ended, and I'm not aware of a single case in which there were any objections, complaints, or protests against those symbols on anyone's part, including persons who were not ethnic Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Let's move to another law. Now, first of all, yesterday you testified I think that -- you said that wherever possible in drafting legislation from the Croatian community, wherever possible you tried to follow the existing provisions, albeit the SFRY legislation or the BiH legislation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that we had tried to stay in line with the regulations of Bosnia and Herzegovina that were valid at the time. I was not talking about the regulations of the former SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Let's look at Exhibit P 01579.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: It's probably somewhere in the front of your binder. Now, this is a March 1993 decree on border crossing and traffic in the border area of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna in times of war and immediate threat of war, and what I'm interested in is Article 1. I think I'll read it out again: "The Law on Border Crossing and Traffic in the Border Area," and there's a reference to the SFRY Official Gazette, "which became part of the Republic's legislature by the Decree with the Force of Law of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, "and there's a reference to the Official Gazette of Bosnia and Herzegovina, "shall apply in the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, provided that its provisions are not in contravention of this Decree or other regulations based on this Decree." Now, I'm interested in that last sentence. Was this a sentence that was often used whenever you would have a decree where you would apply the decree in combination with existing BiH legislation?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can see how the regulations were adopted, this is the usual method, and you can see here that this is a federal regulation, a regulation of the former SFRY, which was first adopted by the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina as its regulation; and then the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna adopted it as a republican regulation. And in the last sentence you can see the legal standard, where it is stipulated that this regulation, which now has the status of a republican regulation, the regulation of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, shall apply with the exception of the articles -- provisions that are in contravention of other articles contained in this decree. In other words, if any article of this adopted law is in collision with any of the articles of this decree, this decree shall have primacy in application. But now that you ask me this, I would like to remind you of Avery important thing, Article 2. I think it's very important because it gives us an answer to the question that we've been discussing over the past days and today, where it is indicated that this space was the territory of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the area of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. This is just a small contribution on my part to this debate about territory and area.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all other microphones in the courtroom be switched off. It appears that somebody's microphone is switched on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Okay. So if I understand your evidence, and I think that's what you said that is based on the language in Article 1, it appears that the regulation -- the provisions of the Croatian community would prevail -- yeah, would prevail over the existing BiH legislation?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if these provisions or regulations were in conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, doesn't that, in other words, mean that the Croatian community by adopting regulations, it could adopt to the extent that it actually suited the Croatian community, and that whatever didn't suit them they would issue a decree or regulation on?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was a relatively short period of time in which a legal system of a country that had broken up had to be adopted, and this system took 50 years to build. In technical terms, in terms of personnel, it was impossible for all the legal instruments, primarily laws of that country, to be analysed and then to take all of those who were unacceptable - and many were unacceptable because they reflected the previous social and political system, social self-government - to change them accordingly. But it was not possible, there was not enough time to amend them by adopting detailed regulations; and this is why this standard was used, stipulating that this is being adopted but that any provisions that are contrary to the key issues regulated by this -- by a given decree shall not apply or that the solutions contained in the given decree shall be given primacy. So this was simply the same method that was used also at the level of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In April 1992, I myself took part in this exercise, where in a single issue of the Official Gazette all of the federal regulations were adopted, the federal regulations that the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina felt should be adopted; and the same legal standard was applied. It was stated that the federal regulations shall apply unless they are in contravention of the relevant republican regulations. So the same legal standard was applied in this decree and in a number of other decrees passed by the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna when the regulations were adopted.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you. Okay. Well, let's move again to another topic which you've touched upon also in -- on Monday and Tuesday, which is the supremacy of the HVO Croatian community over the municipal HVOs. Maybe you can look at Exhibit P 00303. It's an exhibit that you saw before. So this is the statutory decision on the temporary organization of executive authority and administration in the territory of the HZ HB, and I'd like to focus your attention again on Article 14 and 15 which deals with the supremacy of the HVO and which reads: "The HVO shall supervise the work of its departments and municipal HVOs. The HVO may use its supervisory power to annul or abolish individual legal acts passed by the bodies referred to in the foregoing paragraph." Then in Article 15: "In a municipal HVO, if a municipal HVO has passed a decision or performed an act violating the basic legal provisions of the HZ HB, the HVO has the right and duty to dissolve the said municipal HVO. The mandate of all HVO members shall cease on the day the decision to dissolve the separate HVA is issued, and the HVO shall propose members for the new municipal HVO within eight days of having dissolved the old one." I think you testified about this on Monday or Tuesday as well; and from what I understand from your evidence, you were saying, yes, that it's correct that de jure the Croatian community had such powers to supervise the work of the municipalities, but that de facto this was different. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This article created a legal basis for inspections to be carried out by or supervision to be carried out by the HVO. In the period that we're talking about, the situation was different. In reality, this kind of supervision could not be done and it was not done.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: To your knowledge, were ever decisions issued by the HVO, referring to Articles 14 and 15? So, in other words, was there ever a regulation by the municipality annulled or abolished by the Croatian community?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Article 14, paragraph 2, it is stated that the HVO shall have supervisory power of the municipal bodies of the HVO. Individual administrative acts are acts that the municipal authorities pass at the request of natural persons or legal entities. Let us assume that one such act, legal act, was passed at the request of a citizen, of a natural person, and that person is then unhappy with the solutions contained. That person is unhappy with the way that their right is being defined there. There are two models for supervision. One is to control this individual legal act through the mechanism of appeal. If you ascertain that the rights of the citizens have been violated, you as the second-instance body have the power to annul this act or to amend it, to pass your own act, to rectify the situation. The second model that exists in the legal practice of Bosnia-Herzegovina is to supervise, exert supervision, through inspectorates. A citizen can resort to an inspectorate and complain that the municipal authorities violated their rights. For a year and a half, this was my job: You go out, you verify the complaints filed by the citizens, and if you ascertain that they were valid, you take appropriate legal measures, legal remedies, all the way down to the termination of employment of the person who violated the rights of the complainant. When I said it was impossible, in fact, to implement this kind of supervision on the part of the HVO, I was talking about the fact that for a long time the Croatian Defence Council did not have at that level, the level of the HZ HB, inspections, inspectorates, although legal requisites were in place for them to exist. They did not exist, nevertheless, because there were no personnel, trained personnel, who could do this kind of a job. Yesterday, in answer to some of the questions, I said at one point that we saw that when the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna adopted the Law on Administrative Procedures, which made it possible to have a two-instance system and made it possible for the citizens to appeal against the decisions of the municipal authorities, to rectify any errors. And there was also a third possibility, when the HVO HZ HB learnt about some decisions passed by the municipal authorities, which in its opinion were in contravention of the regulations of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and did so sua sponte, I am aware of several such instances when the HVO HZ HB ascertained that the municipal authorities did pass regulations that were in contravention of the regulations of the HZ HB, and then the HVO HZ HB intervened and those decisions passed by the lower-level instances, the municipal HVOs, were then annulled, they were made invalid.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So, looking at the last part of your answer, where the question I put to you was, "Were decisions ever annulled," it seems that you are saying, yes, it did happen that the HVO HZ HB annulled or abolished decisions of municipalities; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Maybe if we can look at P 00431 in your binder. Would you agree with me that this is such a decision which you've just talked about that would render invalid part of a municipality decision? Would this be an example of that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Here, we have an example upon such decision when the HVO intervened and invalidates a decision of a municipal decision or part thereof, the part that the HVO deemed to be unlawful because it is violating the regulations of the HZ HB.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And if we can look at another exhibit which is P 02248, this is a decision on the invalidation of the decision on mobilisation of material-technical goods in the municipality of Mostar, number 01225/93, 24 March 1993, and it's a decision signed by Mr. Prlic. Again, would this also be an example of such a decision?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is one of the several decisions that I know of.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And if I can now ask you to look at Exhibit 1D 01611, that's probably in the back of your binder. These are minutes of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, session 45, held on the 12th of June, 1993, and I'm particularly interested in item number 9: "Discussion on the implementation -- discussion to implement the mobilisation in certain municipalities." If we can go to item 9 which is on page 3 of the English version of the document, let me just read out the first paragraph of item 9: "The head of the defence department HVO HZ HB, Mr. Stojic, informed the session on how the mobilisation was proceeding. The mobilisation was proceeding rather well in certain municipalities (for example, Capljina, Stolac, Bugojno, and Gornji Vakuf), but it was not at the required level in other municipalities (for example, Mostar, Ljubuski, Citluk, Posusje, and Grude). This was the reason to hold meetings in Citluk and Grude and make personnel changes in some municipalities." Then it continues, and then on the conclusions: "1, the decision assigning members of the HVO HZ HB to monitor the implementation of mobilisation in municipalities is hereby amended and reads as follows," and then we get a group of names and then a list. On the next page, I'll read out number 5: "By the end of the week, hold a working meeting with the presidents of the HVO on the implementation of regulations on the territory of the HZ HB." Now, would you agree with me, Mr. Perkovic, that this is an example where you can see that the HVO clearly had supremacy over the municipalities and was very much involved in the operation of the municipalities?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regarding item 9, I don't know what personnel changes are referred to here, but I am absolutely or mostly sure that those were not the decisions of the Croatian Defence Council of the HZ HB and about any personnel changes that were implemented by the HVO HZ HB. Second, we don't see from here that the personnel changes referred to the changes within the municipal Croatian Defence Councils or to personnel changes within the defence offices within the municipalities, and you will agree that these are as different as chalk and cheese. So the issue of personnel changes in the defence offices were not within the jurisdiction of the Croatian Defence Council of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. So this would be my comment regarding Article 9. It is not contested, and this is what I have been repeating in the course of my testimony, that the Croatian Defence Council had various contacts with the heads of the municipal HVOs and that sometimes meetings were held with the leaders of the municipal HVOs. That gave them an opportunity to fix some things, to get a fuller picture, or perhaps to exert pressure on the municipal HVOs to improve their efficiency in performing some tasks. But the HVO HZ HB did not avail itself of the mechanisms contained in the decree that made it possible for them to remove from office the members of the municipal HVOs, and that was not because it was felt that all the municipal HVOs were doing an excellent job. Quite the contrary was the case. The prevailing belief was that it would be a very good thing to perform some changes in some municipal HVOs, but I think that the HVO HZ HB did not have the political power to do so. So there were legal prerequisites to do it, but there was no political power to actually do it at that time simply because the leaders of those municipal HVOs were superior to the HVO on a different basis, by virtue of the fact that they were members of the Presidency of the HZ HB.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Just on item number 5 -- point number 5 under item number 9, when they talk about holding a working meeting with the presidents of the municipal HVOs, did that happen more often, that there would be working meetings with the presidents of municipalities on the implementation of regulations?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What happened most often, what was most often the case, was that some members of the HVO of the HZ HB would meet with the municipal HVO leader. It was customary practice to go out into the field, as the word goes, in a delegation numbering one to three members that would discuss the relevant issues, the issues relevant to that particular municipality, with the municipal leaders. Most often [as interpreted], meetings comprised the entire HVO HZ HB and the municipal HVO on the other side. I do not rule out the possibility that a couple of such meetings took place with the municipal HVO in Mostar, but for the most part the contacts were carried out through a delegation of the HVO HZ HB and the relevant HVO municipal structure or by having a representative of a municipal HVO structure coming to visit the HVO HZ HB.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm told that on the record, page 82, line 15, the gentleman said, "rarely meetings comprised of," as opposed to "most often, meetings comprised." I don't know, I'm told that this is what the gentleman indicated. Perhaps he can repeat that part of his answer, whether it was "most often, meetings comprised the entire HVO HZ HB and municipal HVOs," or "rarely," which of the two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, Witness, do you confirm this point or you don't?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not following the transcript, so I'll repeat. I said that meetings that included the entire HVO HZ HB and the entire HVO municipal structures took place rarely. I only know of a couple of such cases. Most of the time such meetings were held between the delegations of the HVO, on the one hand side, and the municipal HVOs or the leader of the municipal HVO or other important officials of a given HVO municipal structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Mr. Perkovic, let's move again to another topic, and I want to discuss with you briefly now about the HVO camps, and for that I will again refer to part of your testimony in the Kordic case. This is on transcript page 20684 of 7 June 2007, and I'll read out what you said then: "I'm not denying, and I already said that, that at the local level there were such treatments of civilians, non-Croat population. This cannot be justified by war operations, and also there is no for that in the legislation of Herceg-Bosna."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bos, there must be a problem because Mrs. Tomic is standing up. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will not be going into what the testimony of this witness was in the Kordic case; however, in this case, in the examination-in-chief, this topic was not touched upon at all and this is completely beyond the scope of the examination-in-chief. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Bos --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I think, under Rule 90, I'm entitled to visit evidence which is relevant to the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to consult my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Rule 90 stipulates that during cross-examination, you can only refer to points that were broached upon during the direct examination, but a party is entitled to dealing with other matters, and I'm going to read this out to you: "Cross-examination shall be limited to the subject matter of the evidence-in-chief and matter affecting the credibility of the witness, and, where the witness is able to give evidence relevant to the case for the cross-examining party, to the subject matter of that case." It's Article 90 (H), so there's no need for a translation. You can read this in your language, and it states that a party during cross-examination is entitled to asking questions on the basis that points that were dealt with during the direct examination regarding credibility but also for things which are to do with the cause of the party; in this case, it's the indictment. It is broad. You can either interpret this strictly or broadly. I personally interpret this restrictively, but the Chamber interprets this broadly, so you are allowed to ask your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I be allowed to remind you that at one point of my cross-examination, I ventured into dealing with a topic that was not covered by the examination-in-chief, and I also quoted Rule 90 because I deemed that the topic was important, and that in view of the indictment and my case, I was entitled to examine on that topic. The position of the Trial Chamber on that occasion was different. If I may remind you, you invoked the guide-lines and passed a decision that I should not be allowed to cross-examine on this issue; rather, that this would be considered as part of our case and should be deducted from the time of General Petkovic. I believe that the situation we are faced with at present should be dealt with in the same way because we should honour the equality of arms. Since the Prosecutor has already exhausted the time they had for their cross-examination, I think that the same principle should apply as was applied in my case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, let me add one thing. In accordance with Rule 90(H) that you have just referred to, particularly in view of the last paragraph, (ii), it is quite evident that in this case, the Prosecutor should file a request to be allowed to examine on a topic that was not covered by the examination-in-chief and to explain what their case is, and why they believe that in this case they should be allowed to go beyond the scope of cross-examination -- of examination-in-chief. Only once the Prosecutor has stated his reasons will the Trial Chamber be in a position to render a decision on this, though admittedly the Trial Chamber does have the discretionary power to make a ruling, but should first hear the Prosecutor and his argument. The Prosecutor only said that he invokes Rule 90 but did not state his reasons for doing so. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In our ruling the 24th of April, 2008, on the guide-lines, paragraph 7, guide-line number 3, as to the rules governing cross-examination, it is reminded that pursuant to Rule 90, cross-examination may deal with a matter that has not been raised in direct examination, and there is a footnote, decision on the on the mode of interrogating witnesses, the 10th of May, paragraph 13. I disagreed with that paragraph, and this is the reason why paragraph 8 was added, which I'm going to read out to you: "Nonetheless, the cross-examination dealing with a subject not raised in the direct examination is not a cross-examination strictly speaking, but an examination resembling the direct examination." Footnote, decision 10th of May, 2007, paragraph 13: "As a result, the rules applying to direct examination must be respected. Consequently, leading questions shall not be permitted in this type of examination." This means, Mr. Bos, when asking questions on the camps which were not raised during direct examination, you are not entitled to asking leading questions, but you should proceed as if you were carrying out a direct examination. This is what our decision -- our Chamber ruling states on 24th of April, 2008. Well, let's not open this topic because it's time; and in 25 minutes' time, I will have to be in Courtroom III. We shall be resuming tomorrow at 9.00. According to the Registry's calculations, you've used up three hours and 15 minutes. So, roughly speaking, you have an hour and a three-quarters still. So this is what I had to say to conclude today's session. I wish you a good day, and we'll see you tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 4th day of September, 2008, at 9.00 a.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
